lesson.title: Claiming a Port: The Bind Operation
lesson.summary: The bind operation assigns a local socket address to a socket, and it is what lets a server claim a known port in advance so that clients have a fixed address to reach it at.
lesson.body:
bind() is the sockets API call that assigns a local socket address to a socket, telling the operating system that this socket, and only this socket, owns this particular IP address and port combination.

It helps to see why a server needs this while a client usually does not. A client generally does not care which local port it ends up using, since it is the one initiating the conversation, and the operating system can pick an unused ephemeral port automatically the moment connect() is called. A server is in the opposite position: it needs to be reachable at a port that clients already know about in advance, something like port 443 for HTTPS. That means a server has to explicitly call bind() to claim that specific port before it can do anything else, since without a fixed, known address, clients would have no way to find it at all.

The IP address half of bind() matters too. A server can bind to one specific local IP address if the machine has more than one, restricting itself to accepting traffic that arrives on a single network interface, or it can bind to the wildcard address, 0.0.0.0 for IPv4, to accept connections arriving on any of the machine's interfaces at that port.

There is a failure mode worth knowing about: only one socket can be bound to a given IP address and port combination at a time under normal circumstances, so a second attempt to bind() a different socket to a port that is already claimed will fail. This is exactly why restarting a server sometimes produces an address already in use error immediately afterward, until the operating system finishes releasing the previously bound socket.

As a concrete example, a web server calls socket() to create a TCP socket, then calls bind() to attach it to the socket address 0.0.0.0:8080, claiming port 8080 across all of the machine's interfaces before doing anything else. From there it moves on to listen(), the subject of the next chapter, so that it can actually begin accepting client connections at the address it just claimed.
